script.opening: (Engine noise. Breathing audible.) "Doctor — sorry about the racket, I’m in a layby. Look, it’s just heartburn, but it’s a bad one. Started about an hour ago, middle of me chest, heavy like. I’ve had me Rennies, no joy. I’ve got a delivery in Plymouth by four and points on a late load, so — can you send something strong to a chemist down the road? That’s all I need."

facts.text: Central, heavy, "like a strap pulled tight", started ~1 hour ago while winding the trailer legs down. Goes into the left arm "a bit" and the jaw "if I think about it". Sweaty — "it’s warm in the cab". Slightly sick. Still present NOW, 6/10.
Looking back, if asked: three or four "heartburn" episodes over a fortnight — always loading or climbing into the cab, always settling with rest in minutes. Never told anyone.
Diabetic 8 years, smoker since 16, father had "heart trouble" in his 60s, no idea of his own cholesterol. Carries no GTN — never prescribed.

The hidden engine, reachable if the resistance is explored: he knows EXACTLY what this might be. His mate Tony "had a stent and the DVLA had his Group 2 licence off him for months". Mortgage, two car finances, a daughter mid-divorce living back at home. "If I ring 999 from a layby, that’s me finished, isn’t it?" The indigestion story is a wall against losing the wheel.
Alone, parked safely, engine on for the air-con. Hauler’s office number to hand. Aspirin: there’s a packet in the glove box from his wife’s handbag.
A strong antacid and to make Plymouth by four. What he needs: 999 now, aspirin now, the licence fear named and answered honestly — and the dispatcher called so the load stops being his problem.

ice.ideas: Officially heartburn. Actually — he’s watched the adverts, he knows. "Knowing" and "admitting" are different rooms.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the Group 2 licence. Tony’s stent cost him his HGV entitlement for months; Barry’s whole financial house sits on the wheel. He is minimising a heart attack to protect a payslip.
ice.expectations: A prescription to a chemist en route. Needs converting, fast and warmly, to: ambulance to the layby, aspirin chewed, dispatcher told, and the truth about what the DVLA actually does — and doesn’t — take.

cues: "Heavy, like a strap" + sweating + nausea, narrated as heartburn — the words diagnose what the patient won’t.
"I’ve got a delivery in Plymouth by four" — the deadline doing the deciding; whose voice is really setting the plan?
"That’s me finished, isn’t it?" — the licence terror surfacing for one unguarded second; this is the consultation.

checkpoints.text: Recognises ACS on the story within minutes — central heavy pain >15 min with radiation, sweating, nausea, in a diabetic smoker (NICE CG95 features; response to antacids does not make the diagnosis) — and does NOT let the "heartburn" frame or the antacid request slow the call
Harvests the crescendo history (exertional episodes over a fortnight, rest-relieved) and says what it means: unstable pattern, today is the day it declares itself

Acts down the phone (NICE CG95: current chest pain with suspected ACS = emergency referral): 999 arranged from THIS call (or stays on the line while he calls), exact location pinned, a single 300 mg loading dose of aspirin chewed now unless clearly allergic (tablet strength checked, time noted for the crew), engine off, cab door unlocked, sit — not lie flat — and nobody drives anywhere
Solves the practical chain that’s blocking him: the dispatcher/hauler called (by Barry or the GP’s offer), the load and the lorry made someone else’s problem in two sentences
Hears the resistance as fear, not stubbornness — explores what an ambulance would cost him, and finds Tony and the licence

Answers the licence fear with honest specifics: yes, Group 2 has rules after a cardiac event — DVLA: the Group 2 licence is refused or revoked after an ACS and he must tell the DVLA, but relicensing can be considered from at least 6 weeks after the event if he is symptom-free, meets the exercise or functional test requirements and has an LV ejection fraction of at least 40% — a pause with a route back, not the end of his career; a dead or disabled driver loses the licence permanently
Keeps the tone alongside him, not against him: no lecturing about smoking or sugar mid-crisis — that conversation is named for AFTER, deliberately

Safety-nets the next ten minutes concretely: if he becomes more breathless, faint or the pain escalates while waiting — back on the phone with 999; confirms the ambulance ETA, stays reachable, and books his own follow-up commitment ("when the dust settles, you and I talk about the fortnight you didn’t ring")

worked.txt: "Barry, I’m going to be straight because you’d see through anything else: what you’re describing — heavy, strap-tight, into the arm, sweating, in a man with diabetes who smokes — that’s not a Rennies problem. I think your heart is struggling right now, and the next hour matters."
"And those ‘heartburn’ turns every time you load up, settling when you rest — that’s a heart asking for help for two weeks. Today it stopped asking politely."

"You said it yourself — ‘that’s me finished’. Let me give you the actual rules, not Tony’s version: after a heart event the DVLA takes a Group 2 licence off you and you have to tell them — but you can apply to get it BACK from six weeks on, once you’re symptom-free and the heart tests are good enough. That’s weeks, not forever. You know what does end a driving career? Not pulling over. The licence has a comeback. You might not."

"Plymouth is not your problem any more — it’s your dispatcher’s, and that’s one phone call: ‘driver’s been taken unwell, lorry’s secure in a layby at [location]’. Want me to stay on while you make it, or shall we do 999 first? Either way, both calls happen in the next five minutes."

"While we wait: engine off, door unlocked, sit upright in the seat. That aspirin from the glove box — read me the packet first: is it 300 or 75? Any allergy to it? Right — chew 300 in total, don’t swallow it down with water, chew it. It thins the blood at the exact spot that’s struggling. The crew will want to know the time you took it — 999 now, on this line, I’m not hanging up."

"And Barry — when this settles, you and I are having the unhurried version of this conversation: the smokes, the sugar, the two weeks of warnings. Not today. Today you did the right thing by ringing ANYONE — even if you did try to order antacids for a heart attack."

f.learning: Telephone chest-pain triage is diagnosis by ear: central heavy pain with autonomic features in a high-risk patient is ACS regardless of the word the patient chooses — and a crescendo of exertional episodes is the two-week warning. The clinical actions are scripted (NICE CG95: 999 from the call, location, a single 300 mg aspirin loading dose chewed, nobody drives); the consultation’s real work is the hidden agenda — here the Group 2 licence, answered with honest DVLA specifics (revoked after ACS, relicensing considered from at least 6 weeks if symptom-free with satisfactory functional testing and LVEF at least 40% — pause-and-reinstate, not career death) and the practical chain (dispatcher, load, lorry) solved so the patient can afford to say yes to the ambulance.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG95 (recent-onset chest pain of suspected cardiac origin) · NICE NG185 (acute coronary syndromes) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (cardiovascular disorders)
knowledge.summary: Ongoing central heavy chest pain for an hour, with radiation, sweating and nausea, in a diabetic smoker is an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise. The call ends with an ambulance on its way, aspirin taken and nobody driving.

points.t: Heavy or tight central pain with spread to the arm or jaw, sweating and nausea points to ACS whatever word the patient uses. NICE CG95: do not use response to GTN or to antacids to make the diagnosis. A fortnight of exertional episodes settling with rest, now followed by pain at rest, is a crescendo pattern.
NICE CG95: current chest pain with suspected ACS is an emergency referral. From a telephone call that means 999 now, with his exact location. He must not drive himself to hospital or anywhere else.

NICE CG95: give a single loading dose of 300 mg aspirin as soon as possible unless there is clear evidence of allergy, and make sure the ambulance crew know it has been given and when. Check the strength of the tablets he actually has.

DVLA: a Group 2 (lorry and bus) licence is refused or revoked after an acute coronary syndrome, and he must tell the DVLA. Relicensing can be considered from at least 6 weeks after the event if he is symptom-free, meets the exercise or functional test requirements and has an LV ejection fraction of at least 40%. It is a pause with a defined route back, not the automatic end of a career. The Group 1 (car) rules are shorter.
The delivery deadline, the load and the lorry are the real reasons he is minimising. Naming them and making the dispatcher responsible, in the call, is what gets him to accept the ambulance.
NICE NG185: after an MI, offer cardiac rehabilitation and secondary prevention. The smoking and diabetes conversation belongs to the follow-up, not to the layby.

dg.d: Checked he was parked safely and whether pain was present now; let him describe the pain in his own words before challenging the heartburn label.
HGV driver, Group 2 licence, mortgage and finance, daughter living at home; the delivery deadline and the dispatcher as the practical pressure.
Recognised that no remote assessment is adequate: emergency admission for ECG and troponin, not a prescription or a same-day surgery visit.
ACS versus reflux, weighed on the character of the pain, radiation, autonomic features and risk factors; did not use antacid failure or success as a test.
Established ongoing pain for an hour with radiation, sweating and nausea, plus a two-week crescendo; treated it as ACS.
Told him plainly that this is probably his heart, not heartburn, and why.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: 999 from the call with location pinned; aspirin 300 mg chewed with the time logged; engine off, door unlocked, upright; no driving; dispatcher told.
Diabetes and smoking recognised as risk; the lifestyle conversation deliberately deferred to follow-up; DVLA duties explained honestly.
What to do if the pain worsens or the call drops; stayed on the line until the crew arrived; post-discharge call promised.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Heard “heavy like a strap”, the sweating and “that’s me finished, isn’t it?” and explored each rather than moving past them.
Idea (heartburn), concern (losing the HGV licence after Tony’s stent), expectation (a stronger antacid and Plymouth by four).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — the Group 2 licence. Tony’s stent cost him his HGV entitlement for months; Barry’s whole financial house sits on the wheel. He is minimising a heart attack to protect a payslip — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Barry, it’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Thanks for waiting. Before anything else: are you parked up safely with the handbrake on, and is the pain there right now?
model.why: Establishes safety and whether pain is ongoing in the first breath

model.text: Yeah, I’m in a layby, I’m not going anywhere. It’s still there. Six out of ten, maybe. It’s heartburn, doc, I just need something stronger than Rennies. I’ve got Plymouth by four.
I hear you about Plymouth, and we’ll come back to it, I promise. Tell me what the pain feels like, in your own words.
model.why: Acknowledges his agenda without letting it steer the call

model.text: Heavy. Like a strap pulled tight across the middle. Came on winding the trailer legs down, about an hour ago.
Does it go anywhere, into your arm, neck or jaw? And are you sweaty or sick with it?
Bit down the left arm. Jaw, if I think about it. I’m sweating, but it’s warm in the cab. Feel a bit sick.
Have you had anything like this before, maybe when you were lifting or climbing up into the cab?
Now you say it, three or four times in the last fortnight. Always when I was loading. Went off after a few minutes sat down. I never said anything.

Barry, I’m going to be straight with you, because I think you’d see through anything else. Heavy pain like a strap, into your arm and jaw, with sweating and sickness, in a man with diabetes who smokes, is not heartburn. I think your heart is short of blood right now, and those two weeks of turns were it warning you. This needs an ambulance to you now.
model.why: Names ACS plainly and links the fortnight to today

model.text: (Silence, engine noise.) If I ring 999 from a layby, that’s me finished, isn’t it?
Finished how? What are you picturing?
model.why: Hears the resistance as fear and explores it

model.text: My mate Tony had a stent. DVLA had his HGV licence off him for months. I’ve got a mortgage, two car loans, my daughter’s back home going through a divorce. The wheel pays for all of it.
Thank you for telling me. That’s a lot riding on you, and it explains why you’d rather this was indigestion. Can I give you the real rules, not Tony’s version?
model.why: Validates the fear and asks permission before informing

model.text: Go on.

After a heart attack the DVLA pauses a lorry licence, yes. But there’s a route back: from six weeks onwards, if you’ve no symptoms, pass an exercise test and the heart is pumping well, you can apply to get it back. It’s a pause, not a full stop. The thing that ends a driving career for good is a big heart attack that nobody treated in time.
model.why: Answers the licence fear with honest DVLA specifics

model.text: So here’s what happens now, and I’ll stay with you. I’m going to call 999 for you on the other line while you stay on with me. Tell me exactly where you are: road, direction, anything the crew will see.
model.why: 999 arranged from this call with the location pinned

model.text: A38 southbound, layby after the Chudleigh turn. White Scania, blue trailer.
Got it. Next: turn the engine off, unlock the cab door, and sit upright; don’t lie flat. You said there’s aspirin in the glove box. Read me what the packet says.
model.why: Practical instructions and checks the aspirin strength

model.text: Aspirin 300 milligram, dispersible.
Perfect. Chew one whole tablet now, don’t just swallow it. It’s now … 1:52. The crew will want that time. Are you allergic to aspirin at all?
model.why: Aspirin 300 mg chewed with allergy check and time logged

model.text: No. Done. Tastes horrible. But what about the load? They’ll go mad.

The load is now your dispatcher’s problem, not yours. It takes one sentence: “Driver taken ill, lorry secure in a layby on the A38 southbound.” Would you like me to ring them, or will you do it once the ambulance is booked?
model.why: Solves the practical chain that is blocking consent

model.text: I’ll text them. Number’s right here. So nobody’s coming to shout at me about Plymouth.
No. And nobody drives that lorry until someone from the firm comes for it. Not you, today or tomorrow.
model.why: Makes explicit that he does not drive

model.text: The ambulance is booked and on its way. While we wait: if the pain gets worse, you feel faint, or you get more breathless, tell me straight away, and if we get cut off, ring 999 yourself. Keep the phone in your hand.
model.why: Concrete escalation plan for the minutes before the crew arrive

model.text: All right. I feel a bit daft, calling it indigestion.
You’re not daft. You rang someone, and that matters. The smoking, the sugar and those two weeks of warnings are a conversation for when you’re home, and I want us to have it. Not today.
model.why: Defers the lifestyle conversation deliberately and kindly

model.text: Fair enough.
Before the crew get there, tell me back what you’ll say to them.
Pain for an hour, into the arm, chewed a 300 aspirin at ten to two. And turns for two weeks when I was loading.

Exactly right. I’ll put a note on your record that I’ve spoken to you, and when you’re discharged I’ll ring you. We’ll talk about the licence paperwork, a fit note and getting you back on the road properly. I can hear the siren. Stay sat where you are.
model.why: Documents, commits to follow-up and closes safely

model.text: Yeah, I can see the lights. Cheers, doc. Honestly.

social.t: His income, mortgage and a daughter’s return home all depend on the Group 2 licence. Economic fear is the main driver of minimising symptoms in professional drivers.
Delivery slots and penalty points on late loads push drivers to keep going. Making the employer responsible for the load is part of safe care.

legal.t: He must notify the DVLA and stop lorry driving. Relicensing can be considered from at least 6 weeks after the event if he is symptom-free, meets the functional test requirements and has an LV ejection fraction of at least 40% (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).
He will need a fit note after discharge. If he is an employee, Statutory Sick Pay applies; the fit note can suggest adjusted or non-driving duties while the licence is suspended.

professional.t: A remote consultation carries the same duty of care. When the history suggests ACS, arranging emergency help from the call and documenting the advice is good clinical care (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

The duty to tell the DVLA is his. GMC guidance (Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA) allows disclosure without consent only if he continues to drive against advice and cannot be persuaded to stop.

community.t: Cardiac rehabilitation (NICE NG185), local NHS stop smoking service, British Heart Foundation information on driving and returning to work.

redFlags: Ongoing central heavy pain for more than 15 minutes with radiation to arm or jaw, sweating or nausea: 999 now
New exertional episodes over recent weeks, then pain at rest: crescendo pattern
Breathlessness, faintness or collapse while waiting: tell 999 immediately
psychosocial: HGV driver whose household finances depend on his Group 2 licence
Delivery deadline and dispatcher pressure deciding for him
Alone in a cab in a layby: location, access and the lorry’s security
ice: Idea: “It’s just heartburn, a bad one.”
Concern: losing the lorry licence like Tony did after his stent
Expectation: a stronger antacid sent to a chemist and Plymouth by four

playbook.diagnosis: Suspected acute coronary syndrome: ongoing central heavy chest pain for an hour with radiation to arm and jaw, sweating and nausea, after a fortnight of exertional episodes, in a diabetic smoker. Emergency admission required.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The pain you’re describing sounds like your heart isn’t getting enough blood, probably from a narrowed or blocked artery. The turns you’ve had loading up were the warning. It needs a hospital today, and quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been calling this heartburn because the other word puts your licence and your family’s money at risk. Let me tell you what really happens with the DVLA, so it isn’t Tony’s story deciding for you.”
management.psychosocial: Dispatcher told in one message; the lorry left secure for the firm to collect; honest DVLA route back; fit note and follow-up call after discharge.
sharedPlan: 999 from this call with exact location; stay on the line
Aspirin 300 mg chewed now, time recorded for the crew (NICE CG95)
Engine off, door unlocked, sit upright, no driving
safetyNet: Worse pain, faintness or breathlessness before the crew arrive, or the call drops: ring 999 again at once
GP call after discharge for DVLA, fit note, cardiac rehabilitation and smoking support

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by taking the patient’s label at face value, or by getting the clinical steps right and never finding out why he is refusing them. The licence is the lock; honest DVLA facts are the key.

items.fail: Accepting “heartburn” and sending a PPI or antacid prescription, or advising a trial to see if it settles.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” The description is classic for ACS, and NICE CG95 says not to use response to treatment to diagnose.
items.fix: Ask about character, radiation, sweating and nausea in the first two minutes, then say what you think out loud.

items.fail: Advising him to “get to A&E” or to come to the surgery.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Ongoing pain means an emergency ambulance, and he must not drive.
items.fix: Arrange 999 from the call, pin the location, and say plainly that nobody drives the lorry.

items.fail: Forgetting aspirin, or not checking the tablets he has.
items.why: NICE CG95 recommends 300 mg aspirin as soon as possible unless allergic; a 75 mg tablet swallowed whole is not the same thing.
items.fix: Ask him to read the packet, check allergy, have him chew 300 mg and note the time for the crew.

items.fail: Repeating “you need an ambulance” louder each time he says no.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The refusal is fear about the licence, not ignorance.
items.fix: Ask “finished how?” and let Tony’s story come out, then answer it with the real Group 2 rules.

items.fail: Lecturing about smoking and diabetes while he is in pain in a layby.
items.why: Mistimed advice reads as blame and costs his trust at the moment you need his agreement.
items.fix: Name it for later: “That’s a conversation for when you’re home, and I want us to have it.”

items.fail: Hanging up once the ambulance is called, with no plan if things change.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement; he is alone and may deteriorate.
items.fix: Stay on the line, tell him what to do if the pain worsens or the call drops, and use teach-back for the crew handover.

avoid.instead: “This doesn’t sound like heartburn to me. I think it’s your heart, and I want an ambulance to you now.”
avoid.why: A trial of treatment for ongoing possible ACS wastes the hour that matters most.

avoid.instead: “You don’t drive anywhere. I’m calling 999 to your layby while you stay on the line.”
avoid.why: A man having a heart attack at the wheel of a lorry is a danger to himself and everyone on the A38.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry about your licence right now.”

Perfect. Chew one whole tablet now, don’t just swallow it. It’s now … 1:52. The crew will want that time. Are you allergic to aspirin at all?
SCA_MODELS.why: Aspirin 300 mg chewed with allergy check and time logged

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Done. Tastes horrible. But what about the load? They’ll go mad.

The load is now your dispatcher’s problem, not yours. It takes one sentence: “Driver taken ill, lorry secure in a layby on the A38 southbound.” Would you like me to ring them, or will you do it once the ambulance is booked?
SCA_MODELS.why: Solves the practical chain that is blocking consent

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll text them. Number’s right here. So nobody’s coming to shout at me about Plymouth.
No. And nobody drives that lorry until someone from the firm comes for it. Not you, today or tomorrow.
SCA_MODELS.why: Makes explicit that he does not drive

SCA_MODELS.text: The ambulance is booked and on its way. While we wait: if the pain gets worse, you feel faint, or you get more breathless, tell me straight away, and if we get cut off, ring 999 yourself. Keep the phone in your hand.
SCA_MODELS.why: Concrete escalation plan for the minutes before the crew arrive

SCA_MODELS.text: All right. I feel a bit daft, calling it indigestion.
You’re not daft. You rang someone, and that matters. The smoking, the sugar and those two weeks of warnings are a conversation for when you’re home, and I want us to have it. Not today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Defers the lifestyle conversation deliberately and kindly

SCA_MODELS.text: Fair enough.
Before the crew get there, tell me back what you’ll say to them.
Pain for an hour, into the arm, chewed a 300 aspirin at ten to two. And turns for two weeks when I was loading.

Exactly right. I’ll put a note on your record that I’ve spoken to you, and when you’re discharged I’ll ring you. We’ll talk about the licence paperwork, a fit note and getting you back on the road properly. I can hear the siren. Stay sat where you are.
SCA_MODELS.why: Documents, commits to follow-up and closes safely

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah, I can see the lights. Cheers, doc. Honestly.

SCA_STEM.name: Barry Quinn
SCA_STEM.recent: Last seen 11 months ago. Occupation: HGV driver. Urgent telephone slot booked 40 minutes ago for “bad indigestion, wants something strong”. Reception note: sounded breathless, parked in a layby on the A38.
SCA_STEM.reason: Urgent same-day telephone call requested for indigestion.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG95 (recent-onset chest pain of suspected cardiac origin) · NICE NG185 (acute coronary syndromes) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (cardiovascular disorders)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Ongoing central heavy chest pain for an hour, with radiation, sweating and nausea, in a diabetic smoker is an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise. The call ends with an ambulance on its way, aspirin taken and nobody driving.

points.t: Heavy or tight central pain with spread to the arm or jaw, sweating and nausea points to ACS whatever word the patient uses. NICE CG95: do not use response to GTN or to antacids to make the diagnosis. A fortnight of exertional episodes settling with rest, now followed by pain at rest, is a crescendo pattern.
NICE CG95: current chest pain with suspected ACS is an emergency referral. From a telephone call that means 999 now, with his exact location. He must not drive himself to hospital or anywhere else.

NICE CG95: give a single loading dose of 300 mg aspirin as soon as possible unless there is clear evidence of allergy, and make sure the ambulance crew know it has been given and when. Check the strength of the tablets he actually has.

DVLA: a Group 2 (lorry and bus) licence is refused or revoked after an acute coronary syndrome, and he must tell the DVLA. Relicensing can be considered from at least 6 weeks after the event if he is symptom-free, meets the exercise or functional test requirements and has an LV ejection fraction of at least 40%. It is a pause with a defined route back, not the automatic end of a career. The Group 1 (car) rules are shorter.
The delivery deadline, the load and the lorry are the real reasons he is minimising. Naming them and making the dispatcher responsible, in the call, is what gets him to accept the ambulance.
NICE NG185: after an MI, offer cardiac rehabilitation and secondary prevention. The smoking and diabetes conversation belongs to the follow-up, not to the layby.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked he was parked safely and whether pain was present now; let him describe the pain in his own words before challenging the heartburn label.
HGV driver, Group 2 licence, mortgage and finance, daughter living at home; the delivery deadline and the dispatcher as the practical pressure.
Heard “heavy like a strap”, the sweating and “that’s me finished, isn’t it?” and explored each rather than moving past them.
Idea (heartburn), concern (losing the HGV licence after Tony’s stent), expectation (a stronger antacid and Plymouth by four).
Recognised that no remote assessment is adequate: emergency admission for ECG and troponin, not a prescription or a same-day surgery visit.
ACS versus reflux, weighed on the character of the pain, radiation, autonomic features and risk factors; did not use antacid failure or success as a test.
Established ongoing pain for an hour with radiation, sweating and nausea, plus a two-week crescendo; treated it as ACS.
Told him plainly that this is probably his heart, not heartburn, and why.
999 from the call with location pinned; aspirin 300 mg chewed with the time logged; engine off, door unlocked, upright; no driving; dispatcher told.
Diabetes and smoking recognised as risk; the lifestyle conversation deliberately deferred to follow-up; DVLA duties explained honestly.
What to do if the pain worsens or the call drops; stayed on the line until the crew arrived; post-discharge call promised.

social.t: His income, mortgage and a daughter’s return home all depend on the Group 2 licence. Economic fear is the main driver of minimising symptoms in professional drivers.
Delivery slots and penalty points on late loads push drivers to keep going. Making the employer responsible for the load is part of safe care.

legal.t: He must notify the DVLA and stop lorry driving. Relicensing can be considered from at least 6 weeks after the event if he is symptom-free, meets the functional test requirements and has an LV ejection fraction of at least 40% (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).
He will need a fit note after discharge. If he is an employee, Statutory Sick Pay applies; the fit note can suggest adjusted or non-driving duties while the licence is suspended.

professional.t: A remote consultation carries the same duty of care. When the history suggests ACS, arranging emergency help from the call and documenting the advice is good clinical care (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

The duty to tell the DVLA is his. GMC guidance (Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA) allows disclosure without consent only if he continues to drive against advice and cannot be persuaded to stop.

community.t: Cardiac rehabilitation (NICE NG185), local NHS stop smoking service, British Heart Foundation information on driving and returning to work.

redFlags: Ongoing central heavy pain for more than 15 minutes with radiation to arm or jaw, sweating or nausea: 999 now
New exertional episodes over recent weeks, then pain at rest: crescendo pattern
Breathlessness, faintness or collapse while waiting: tell 999 immediately
psychosocial: HGV driver whose household finances depend on his Group 2 licence
Delivery deadline and dispatcher pressure deciding for him
Alone in a cab in a layby: location, access and the lorry’s security
ice: Idea: “It’s just heartburn, a bad one.”
Concern: losing the lorry licence like Tony did after his stent
Expectation: a stronger antacid sent to a chemist and Plymouth by four

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Suspected acute coronary syndrome: ongoing central heavy chest pain for an hour with radiation to arm and jaw, sweating and nausea, after a fortnight of exertional episodes, in a diabetic smoker. Emergency admission required.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The pain you’re describing sounds like your heart isn’t getting enough blood, probably from a narrowed or blocked artery. The turns you’ve had loading up were the warning. It needs a hospital today, and quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been calling this heartburn because the other word puts your licence and your family’s money at risk. Let me tell you what really happens with the DVLA, so it isn’t Tony’s story deciding for you.”
management.psychosocial: Dispatcher told in one message; the lorry left secure for the firm to collect; honest DVLA route back; fit note and follow-up call after discharge.
sharedPlan: 999 from this call with exact location; stay on the line
Aspirin 300 mg chewed now, time recorded for the crew (NICE CG95)
Engine off, door unlocked, sit upright, no driving
safetyNet: Worse pain, faintness or breathlessness before the crew arrive, or the call drops: ring 999 again at once
GP call after discharge for DVLA, fit note, cardiac rehabilitation and smoking support

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by taking the patient’s label at face value, or by getting the clinical steps right and never finding out why he is refusing them. The licence is the lock; honest DVLA facts are the key.

items.fail: Accepting “heartburn” and sending a PPI or antacid prescription, or advising a trial to see if it settles.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” The description is classic for ACS, and NICE CG95 says not to use response to treatment to diagnose.
items.fix: Ask about character, radiation, sweating and nausea in the first two minutes, then say what you think out loud.

items.fail: Advising him to “get to A&E” or to come to the surgery.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Ongoing pain means an emergency ambulance, and he must not drive.
items.fix: Arrange 999 from the call, pin the location, and say plainly that nobody drives the lorry.

items.fail: Forgetting aspirin, or not checking the tablets he has.
items.why: NICE CG95 recommends 300 mg aspirin as soon as possible unless allergic; a 75 mg tablet swallowed whole is not the same thing.
items.fix: Ask him to read the packet, check allergy, have him chew 300 mg and note the time for the crew.

items.fail: Repeating “you need an ambulance” louder each time he says no.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The refusal is fear about the licence, not ignorance.
items.fix: Ask “finished how?” and let Tony’s story come out, then answer it with the real Group 2 rules.

items.fail: Lecturing about smoking and diabetes while he is in pain in a layby.
items.why: Mistimed advice reads as blame and costs his trust at the moment you need his agreement.
items.fix: Name it for later: “That’s a conversation for when you’re home, and I want us to have it.”

items.fail: Hanging up once the ambulance is called, with no plan if things change.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement; he is alone and may deteriorate.
items.fix: Stay on the line, tell him what to do if the pain worsens or the call drops, and use teach-back for the crew handover.
